data.title: Micron stock is highly undervalued as the Wyckoff Theory takes shape
data.description:
Micron stock has slipped into a bear market this month and now appears to be in the Wyckoff theory's markdown phase, even as its key valuation metric has fallen to bargain levels. MU was trading at $601, about 52% below its year-high. So, is this a good time to buy the dip, or should investors sell the rip?

Micron stock has become highly undervalued

In theory, companies that are seeing substantial revenue and profit growth should receive premium valuations. Some of the most popular companies that have always had a premium valuation are Walmart, Costco, and Shopify. 

Micron, however, is doing the opposite. Its revenue growth is soaring, and analysts expect the momentum will continue. The most recent results showed that its fourth-quarter revenue jumped by 379% to $54.2 billion, with its annual figure hitting $133.2 billion. Most of this growth was in its DRAM division, which made $39.8 billion. 

Micron is also a highly profitable company, with the gross margin of all its businesses being over 80%. Its total gross profit margin rose to 87%, much higher than most companies, including Nvidia. 

Most importantly, analysts believe that the company has more room for growth. For example, the first-quarter revenue is expected to hit $61 billion, while the second-quarter figure will soar to $66 billion. Its annual revenue is expected to jump by 106% to $275 billion. 

For a company experiencing this growth, its valuation metrics are significantly low. For example, the forward price-to-earnings ratio stands at just 3.43, much lower than the sector median of 18. 

Similarly, the company has one of the highest rule-of-40 metrics. This multiple is calculated by adding its revenue growth and its profit margins. Micron has a forward revenue growth of 106% and a profit margin of 64%, giving it a multiple of 170%. 

These metrics explain why the company is planning to accelerate its share repurchases in the near term. Its plan is to start a $35 billion program in December when the buyback restrictions end. Share buybacks help to boost a company’s earnings per share by reducing its outstanding shares.

Micron is facing risks

Therefore, the falling Micron stock price and cheaper valuation is happening because of the rising risks in the industry. One of the main risks is that the AI bubble may burst soon. The AI Stock Bubble Index has remained above 60.

There are also concerns that some AI data center companies will find it hard to survive as financing in the industry dries out. Elon Musk has warned that over 200 neocloud companies will collapse.

These fears have risen after the recent Anthropic IPO, in which the company raised over $100 billion. Its stock has plunged afterwards. OpenAI has also struggled in its fundraising. It recently raised $11 billion, much lower the $30 billion it was aiming for. 

There is also a risk that the memory supercycle will end in the coming months or years. Historically, this business is usually made up of major boom-and-bust cycles.

READ MORE: Micron, SanDisk continue their bloodbath; how long will the pain continue?

Micron share price is in the markdown phase

MU stock chart | Source: TradingView

The weekly chart shows that MU stock has formed the classic Wyckoff Method. It remained in a consolidation phase for years, a sign that it was in the accumulation phase. 

The stock then entered the markup phase mid-last year and then started its upward trend, eventually reaching a record high of $1,255. Now, there are signs that it has dropped into the markdown phase, which is characterized by panic selling.

Therefore, the stock will likely continue falling in the near term. The next key level to watch will be at the 50-week moving average of $523.

data.title: Missed the Anthropic IPO? Is now a better time to buy the stock?
data.description:
Anthropic stock (NASDAQ: ANT) climbed 4.7% to $86.69 in early premarket trading on Friday, recovering above their initial public offering price after a volatile first week on Wall Street.

The developer of Claude began trading at $111.50 on 19 November, but concerns about artificial intelligence spending and technology valuations have since pushed its shares more than 22% below that level.

Investors who missed the listing can now buy the stock at just 4.4% above its $83 offering price.

However, independent valuations suggest the discount to its opening trade may offer less protection than investors might expect.

Is Anthropic stock actually cheap after its IPO sell-off?

At Friday's premarket price, Anthropic's market capitalisation is roughly $1.16 trillion, rising to $1.58 trillion when including outstanding and reserved employee equity awards.

Canaccord Genuity, which initiated coverage with a Buy rating and a $135 price target this week, expects revenue of $55.2 billion in 2026, $136.4 billion in 2027 and $224.5 billion in 2028.

Based on those projections, Anthropic trades at approximately 29 times estimated 2026 revenue and seven times projected 2028 sales on a fully diluted basis.

Analysts led by David Hynes Jr. believe autonomous AI agents could capture spending traditionally allocated to corporate labour, expanding Anthropic's potential market beyond enterprise software, according to Investing.com.

Morningstar's Malik Ahmed Khan offers a more restrained assessment. His $92 fair value estimate implies upside of just 6%, while Morningstar's $188 bull case and $25 bear case imply 117% upside and 71% downside.

Finance professor Aswath Damodaran's option-adjusted intrinsic valuation of $76.98, published before the listing, suggests the shares remain expensive even after their recent decline.

Can Anthropic stock's explosive growth justify its valuation?

Anthropic's third-quarter revenue surged to $17 billion from $1.4 billion a year earlier, according to its IPO prospectus, while its reported operating loss narrowed from $3.1 billion to $567 million.

Adjusted operating income reached $2.5 billion, although the corresponding margin declined to 15% from 19% in the preceding quarter.

The company attributed much of that deterioration to $5 billion in relatively expensive short-term computing capacity, highlighting the challenges of expanding infrastructure quickly enough to meet rising demand.

Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate reached $81 billion at the end of October, compared with $71 billion a month earlier.

The metric extrapolates recent customer spending rather than representing guaranteed annual revenue.

Competition from OpenAI, Google and open-weight models could also put pressure on pricing, making sustained profitability harder to achieve even if demand continues growing.

Anthropic's $900 billion commitments are the biggest test

Anthropic has disclosed $900.9 billion in purchase and lease commitments, predominantly related to computing infrastructure, including $451.6 billion through 2030.

Approximately $70.7 billion falls due within 12 months of September 2026. Additional arrangements without fixed spending commitments could cost an estimated $150 billion to $175 billion.

However, these obligations are not equivalent to debt, and Anthropic has substantial financial resources.

The company held $95.6 billion in cash and $36.3 billion in short-term investments at September's end.

It subsequently raised approximately $91.6 billion in gross primary IPO proceeds and another $26 billion through a concurrent private placement.

Operating cash flow reached $6.6 billion in the first nine months of 2026, positive but modest relative to the scale of its infrastructure obligations.

The immediate concern is therefore less about liquidity than whether future customer spending can justify the capacity Anthropic has contracted.

data.title: CMC Markets profit more than doubles to £106M on record first half
data.description:
CMC Markets has reported a record first half, with pre-tax profit more than doubling as its business-to-business (B2B) and institutional arms offset subdued market volatility.

The London-listed broker said profit before tax rose 115% to £106.0 million in the six months to September 30, 2026, from £49.3 million a year earlier, according to its interim results published on November 26, 2026.

Net operating income climbed 54% to £286.6 million, from £186.2 million. CMC said that beat its previous first-half record of £230.9 million, set in HY2021.

Trading revenue leads the gains

Net trading revenue rose 67% to £230.9 million and now makes up about 81% of group income, up from 74%, the company said. The institutional channel showed the fastest growth.

CMC said the record came even though the VIX volatility index stayed below its historical average for most of the period, unlike the more volatile first half of the previous year.

Net investing revenue increased 8% to £28.3 million, while net interest income rose 28% to £25.6 million, helped by active management of group and client cash.

Its Australian stockbroking business posted another record half, with net operating income up 5% to A$69.2 million.

Costs rise more slowly than income

Operating expenses rose 31% to £177.6 million, reflecting higher variable pay, expansion and technology spending, CMC said. Excluding variable remuneration, costs were £152.5 million, up from £128.4 million.

That lifted the pre-tax margin to 37.0% from 26.5%. EBITDA more than doubled to £116.5 million, and basic earnings per share rose to 29.0p from 13.3p.

The board declared a record interim dividend of 10.1p a share, up 84% from 5.5p.

CMC also completed its first £250 million Euro Medium Term Note (EMTN) issue in August, which it said was significantly oversubscribed.

Big partnerships still to come

The broker reiterated its upgraded FY2027 guidance of net operating income of at least £550 million and EBITDA of £250 million. Its financial year ends in March.

CMC said its Westpac stockbroking deal is now expected to launch in the first half of FY2028. Once live, it is expected to be the group’s largest partnership of its kind.

Staff accounts for the ASB partnership in New Zealand are live for end-to-end testing, with launch expected imminently. CMC has also expanded a deal with an unnamed neobank to provide liquidity for CFDs and other derivatives in the UK.

Dubai, warrants and crypto

CMC said its Dubai business doubled revenue between FY2025 and FY2026 and is now its fourth global hub, alongside the UK, Australia and Singapore. It has applied for expanded regulatory permissions there.

Its European warrants business has issued about 8,000 products. CMC plans an Australian warrants pilot trade before the end of 2026, having signed agreements with ASX, BNP Paribas and others.

After the period end, CMC was approved by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) as a cryptoasset business under the UK’s Money Laundering Regulations, the results statement said.

The broker has also added fractional investing, 24/5 trading in US equities and global indices, and wider options coverage to its trading platform.

“Achieving this performance against exceptionally subdued market volatility is particularly significant,” chief executive Lord Cruddas said.

“It demonstrates how far we have moved beyond a business whose performance is principally driven by the retail trading cycle,” he added. Cruddas said his recent personal share purchases of about £5 million “should underline that confidence to the market”.

CMC’s next scheduled update is its FY2027 results in June 2027.

data.title: AMD, Intel, Broadcom rally in premarket trading Friday as AI stocks rebound
data.description:
Chip stocks were rallying in premarket trading on Friday as investors bought the dip following the Thanksgiving holiday.

Intel and AMD gained roughly 4% and Broadcom jumped 3% in early premarket trading at 6:45 AM ET.

All three stocks, alongside major names in the artificial intelligence trade, have been under pressure in recent weeks, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq briefly entering bear-market territory in the previous session.

Intel had shed 0.6% on Wednesday to close at $54.47, AMD had lost 1.75% to $406 while Broadcom stayed almost flat at $300.86.

The broader market was also looking set to jump, with futures linked to all three major indexes rising ahead of the shortened trading session to close the week.

However, with fundamental questions around the sustainability of the AI trade still looming, analysts are unsure whether the rebound will be durable.

"The recovery in stocks seems technical. The questions that caused the market panic are still unanswered," Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB, told Reuters. "If these gains can be sustained on Friday, it would suggest that enthusiasm for the AI trade is back."

There have nevertheless been some positive developments for individual chipmakers that could help support sentiment.

Intel gets two important customer wins

Intel has secured two important customer developments that could support its manufacturing ambitions.

CEO Lip-Bu Tan announced Thursday that the company had signed its first external customer for its advanced 18A-P chip manufacturing process.

Intel has not disclosed the customer's identity, but the agreement marks progress in its effort to compete with Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

Separately, Microsoft became the first publicly named customer for Intel Foundry's EMIB advanced packaging technology, which will be used for Microsoft's Azure first-party silicon.

AMD jumps from Hunterbrook-triggered selloff

AMD has also made progress in its efforts to secure a larger share of the AI infrastructure market even as it struggles with allegations of links with blacklisted Chinese firms.

On November 16, AI infrastructure provider TensorWave announced a six-year agreement with OpenAI to supply 457 megawatts of dedicated computing capacity across multiple US data-center locations.

AMD has also completed its acquisitions of AI research startup World Labs, led by Fei-Fei Li, and specialised inference-chip developer Taalas.

China’s extension of the pause in controls on critical minerals till January is another good news for chipmakers, even though it is only a short-term relief.

Minerals like gallium and germanium are critical inputs in semiconductor manufacturing.

Analysts also remain bullish on the stock with TipRanks data showing 27 out of 30 analysts keeping a 'buy' rating and three suggesting 'hold'.

Broadcom has a major Anthropic deal

Broadcom has also faced significant pressure recently and investors chipped in on Friday to buy the stock, pushing it up before the opening bell.

It recently secured a significant development in its AI business through a financing arrangement involving some of Wall Street's biggest financial institutions.

Bank of America, Blackstone, Citi and Morgan Stanley announced a $63 billion financing structure in October to fund the purchase of Broadcom's custom AI accelerators and networking equipment for Anthropic.

Several Wall Street firms, including StoneX, UBS, and Rosenblatt have reiterated their Buy ratings on Broadcom, but some like Rothschild Redburn have also downgraded the stock with concerns over AI financing and the sustainability of earnings.

Broadcom is scheduled to report its fourth-quarter and full-year 2026 financial results on December 9, giving investors another opportunity to assess whether its AI business can sustain growth despite recent concerns about chip demand.

data.title: Adidas, Puma stocks fall as JPMorgan downgrades both on 2027 outlook
data.description:
Adidas and Puma shares fell on Friday after JPMorgan downgraded both German sportswear makers as part of its 2027 sector outlook, citing slowing industry growth, intensifying competition and limited scope for further gains.

Adidas shares were down more than 2%, while Puma declined about 1.7%.

JPMorgan lowered its price target on Adidas by 20% to €184 from €230, with analyst Chiara Battistini cutting the stock's rating from Buy to Neutral.

The revised target implies about 9% upside from Friday's trading levels.

Separately, analyst Wendy Liu downgraded Puma to Underweight from Neutral and reduced the price target to €21 from €26.

Adidas shares are up more than 1% year to date, while Puma has advanced over 5%.

JPMorgan questions Adidas' growth prospects

JPMorgan said it was becoming more difficult to support Adidas's target of high-single-digit sales growth in 2027 without clearer evidence that its major product franchises could expand further.

The brokerage pointed to lifestyle franchise Stan Smith and running lines Hyperboost and Supernova, saying their ability to scale would be important in sustaining growth.

While the firm remains optimistic about Adidas's apparel business, it sees limited scope for additional upside against a challenging comparable base.

Direct-to-consumer sales have been a bright spot, but JPMorgan warned that growth in the channel could become more expensive in the fourth quarter and into 2027 if the company relies increasingly on promotions.

The brokerage also cautioned that Adidas's current targets of high-single-digit revenue growth and a double-digit operating margin in 2027 leave little room for disappointment in a volatile market.

JPMorgan's fiscal 2027 and fiscal 2028 estimates are high-single-digit and double-digit percentages below consensus, respectively.

The downgrade follows Adidas's latest quarterly results last month, which showed net profit rising to €706 million ($787.4 million) for the quarter ended September, from €461 million a year earlier.

The company also confirmed preliminary sales of €7.25 billion and operating profit of €1.01 billion.

JPMorgan had described the results as reassuring, although it flagged weakness in wholesale footwear sales in Europe.

Adidas maintained its upgraded 2026 guidance, which calls for operating profit of around €2.5 billion and currency-neutral revenue growth of between 9% and 10%.

Puma faces tougher market conditions despite inventory progress

JPMorgan's downgrade of Puma reflects concerns about the broader sportswear industry's growth outlook and the company's ability to regain momentum amid intensifying competition.

However, Puma's recent results have offered some encouragement about its restructuring efforts.

The company reported third-quarter sales of €1.77 billion, down 5% year over year but slightly above analysts' average estimate of €1.75 billion.

Inventories declined 24.3% to €1.6 billion, reflecting lower purchasing volumes.

The reduction has reassured investors about Puma's efforts to normalise stock levels and improve its cost structure, as well as its partnership with Chinese retail giant Anta Sports.

UBS analysts said investors should find the results reassuring, as they suggest Puma remains on track to normalise inventory levels by the end of the year despite a challenging market environment.

Puma also narrowed its 2026 operating result guidance to a loss of between €80 million and €130 million, compared with its previous range of a loss of €50 million to €150 million.

However, questions remain about how quickly the company can return to growth.

Deutsche Bank said in a note to clients after the earnings release: "We need to see more confidence on the 2027 and mid-term outlook at some stage."

The latest downgrades suggest that investors may have to look beyond inventory improvements and near-term earnings resilience when assessing the two sportswear companies.

Their ability to sustain sales growth, protect margins and strengthen their product franchises will be critical as the industry heads into 2027.

data.title: Is Nvidia stock Wall Street's biggest Black Friday bargain?
data.description:
Nvidia stock (NASDAQ: NVDA) climbed 4.7% in premarket trading on Friday as investors returned to beaten-down artificial intelligence stocks.

The chipmaker closed Wednesday at $149.30, more than 37% below its October record high, despite reporting quarterly revenue growth of 103% earlier this month.

The sell-off has left Nvidia trading at just nine times its projected earnings for the next fiscal year, while several Wall Street brokerages have upgraded the stock following Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as chief executive.

Nvidia stock trades at just nine times next year's earnings

Analysts expect Nvidia to generate adjusted earnings of $9.67 per share in fiscal 2027 and $16.61 in fiscal 2028, according to S&P Global estimates.

Based on Wednesday’s close, Nvidia trades at 15.4 times its current fiscal year's projected earnings and nine times those expected the following year.

The discount becomes particularly striking when compared with other semiconductor companies.

On a forward price-to-earnings basis, Stock Analysis puts Nvidia’s multiple at 10.3, compared with 17.3 for Broadcom and 26.9 for Advanced Micro Devices.

Melius Research upgraded Nvidia to Buy from Hold this week, raising its price target from $185 to $220.

Analyst Ben Reitzes said Huang’s return alleviated concerns about supplier relationships, product development and employee retention.

His revised target reflects approximately ten times projected fiscal 2029 earnings, a multiple he described as “still well below Nvidia’s historical averages” in a note published by Price Target.

Applying an illustrative multiple of 15 to consensus fiscal 2028 earnings would value Nvidia at approximately $249 per share, implying 67% upside.

However, reaching that valuation would require both Nvidia meeting earnings expectations and investors becoming willing to pay a higher multiple for those profits.

NVDA stock price: Can Nvidia deliver growth Wall Street expects?

Nvidia’s latest financial results offer considerable evidence that demand for its computing platforms remains strong.

Third-quarter revenue reached $115.8 billion, with data centre sales climbing 110% to $107.6 billion. GAAP operating profit increased 115% to $77.5 billion.

The company forecasts fourth-quarter revenue of approximately $130 billion, excluding data centre compute sales from China.

While that represents sequential growth of 12.3%, the quarter contains an additional reporting week. On an average weekly basis, the projected increase is a more modest 4.2%.

The longer-term outlook remains considerably stronger, with management anticipating revenue growth of approximately 75% in fiscal 2028.

Nvidia has also begun shipping its next-generation Vera Rubin computing systems, with deployments across major cloud providers, including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Oracle.

However, the product transition is putting pressure on profitability.

Nvidia expects adjusted gross margins of between 71% and 72% this quarter, compared with 74.9% in the previous period.

Management anticipates margins will subsequently recover to between 72% and 73% in fiscal 2028, although that would still leave profitability below recent levels.

Could Nvidia's Black Friday bargain become a value trap?

Huang’s reinstatement has not resolved all the concerns surrounding Nvidia’s corporate governance or its increasingly complex financial involvement in the AI infrastructure industry.

S&P Global Ratings placed Nvidia’s AA credit rating on CreditWatch Negative on Wednesday, citing management and governance risks.

Meanwhile, the company’s combined cloud service agreements and data centre lease commitments reached $102 billion last quarter, up from $74 billion three months earlier.

Although these arrangements support Nvidia’s research and development activities, they also underline the scale of its financial commitments to the wider AI ecosystem.

Not every Wall Street analyst is convinced that Huang’s return warrants a more bullish recommendation.

Truist Securities analyst William Stein reiterated his Hold rating and $174 price target on Tuesday, according to Price Target.

Should fiscal 2028 earnings estimates fall by 20%, valuing Nvidia at eight times those revised profits would imply a share price of approximately $106, nearly 29% below Wednesday’s close.

Nvidia’s valuation makes it a compelling Black Friday candidate among major semiconductor stocks, particularly if the anticipated earnings growth materialises.

But investors should distinguish between buying a stock at a discount and buying earnings that may themselves prove overly optimistic.

data.title: Opinion: Oil's surplus will not erase the Hormuz risk premium
data.description:
Oil has had a poor month for bulls and a good week. Brent futures settled at $96.57 a barrel on Thursday, their highest since November 6, and are heading for a first weekly gain in four weeks, according to Reuters and CNBC.

The comfortable view is that the war premium is draining away as Gulf barrels return. I think that is premature. My argument is that the International Energy Agency's surplus is a forecast, while the Strait of Hormuz is a physical constraint. The market is right to keep Brent in the $90s until it eases.

Consider this week's events. On Wednesday, the Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked Ras Tanura, Saudi Arabia's largest refinery and a major export hub.

On Thursday, a projectile struck Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery, halting some operations and killing a Nepalese worker, the Saudi Energy Ministry said.

Iran's Revolutionary Guards also said two tankers hit sea mines north of Oman's Khasab port, one carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude. Early reports described that claim as unverified.

Flows tell the same story. Kpler data show Hormuz clearance averaged 9.25 million barrels a day in the seven days to November 24, about 54% of the pre-war 17.14 million, The National reported.

The strongest counterargument deserves a fair hearing. On November 13, the IEA said global supply would exceed demand by 1.7 million barrels a day in the fourth quarter, the first surplus since the Iran war began. It put the 2027 surplus at about 3.8 million.

Prices have already responded: North Sea Dated crude fell 32% from $136 on October 8 to about $93, the agency said. High prices have also destroyed demand, which the IEA expects to fall by 2.7 million barrels a day this year.

A market that long of oil, the bears say, should not pay a war premium.

We see three reasons to be sceptical. First, the surplus depends on Gulf exports continuing to recover. The IEA itself lists attacks on shipping as a downside risk, and this week showed how quickly it can return.

Second, products are tighter than crude. The IEA calls diesel supply the market's overriding concern, with Gulf product exports roughly half pre-war levels. European diesel futures have fallen almost 30% from their wartime peak, Bloomberg reported, so the squeeze is easing, not over.

Third, the cushion is thin. Rory Johnston of Commodity Context pointed to “known, acute risk” to roughly 15% of global supply and said Brent was oversold below $90. ANZ analysts think it can still push above $100 without another major escalation, though that requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply.

OPEC+ offers little help. Ministers meet on Sunday and may roll over output targets for at least the first quarter of 2027, two people with knowledge of the talks told Reuters. The UAE has left the group, and Iraq and Kazakhstan are pressing for higher capacity estimates.

The stakes reach beyond energy stocks. Futures imply a 99% chance of a Federal Reserve rate rise in December, according to Reuters, and oil in the $90s makes that central bank's task harder, not easier.

For investors, the implication is volatility rather than a clean trend. We expect surplus data to cap rallies when tankers move freely, and Gulf headlines to drive spikes when they do not. Even after its fall, Dated Brent was still $22 above pre-war levels, the IEA said. This is analysis, not a recommendation.

What to watch next? Sunday's OPEC+ decision, and whether Kpler's Hormuz clearance climbs back above 9.25 million barrels a day. Watch the IEA's next monthly report for any change to its surplus forecast, and diesel prices for signs that product tightness is easing.

Also watch the Fed meeting on December 8-9, 2026, where oil's pass-through to inflation will be on the table.

The test of this view is simple. If Brent falls back below $90 while Hormuz flows are still near half of pre-war levels, we are wrong.

data.title: Brent crude price analysis: is November's oil sell-off nearing an end?
data.description:
Oil prices held near a three-week high on Friday as fresh threats to Middle Eastern exports put Brent on course for its first weekly gain in four weeks, challenging the supply-glut narrative that drove November's sell-off.

Brent futures traded at $96.61 a barrel at 04:50 GMT, little changed after Thursday's near-$2 advance.

West Texas Intermediate stood near $85.78, up about 2.5% from Wednesday's settlement because US Thanksgiving interrupted normal trading.

The recovery comes before Sunday's OPEC+ meeting, with traders weighing renewed attacks on shipping and energy facilities against rising production and inventories elsewhere.

Oil prices today: Gulf disruptions challenge hopes of smooth recovery

November's decline reflected a rebound in Gulf exports as producers diverted shipments through pipelines, used escorted tankers and found alternative routes around the Strait of Hormuz.

But further attacks on vessels and Saudi energy infrastructure have raised doubts about whether those arrangements can maintain flows.

Disruptions to refineries and maritime transport may also increase fuel and freight costs without necessarily removing an equivalent volume of crude production.

Giovanni Staunovo, a UBS commodities strategist, said in analysis reported by Barron's this week that the market had concentrated on October's export recovery while overlooking a subsequent decline in Gulf shipments.

That helps explain why a new geopolitical premium is emerging even though October's increase in exports was substantial.

The issue is not simply how much oil is produced, but whether it can reach customers when needed.

Brent crude price analysis: Inventories reveal gap between supply and availability

The International Energy Agency recorded a 52 million-barrel increase in observed global oil inventories during October, supporting expectations that supply is catching up with demand.

Yet oil held at sea grew by 86 million barrels while onshore stocks continued to fall. The latter remain at their lowest levels since at least 2016, the agency said.

Crude in transit cannot always substitute for readily deliverable supplies.

The distinction is visible in the futures market: prompt Brent backwardation, where nearby contracts command a premium over later deliveries, has widened to almost $4 a barrel.

ANZ analysts Brian Martin and Daniel Hynes argued in Friday's research that Brent could move back above $100 without further major escalation, provided evidence of constrained deliverable supply strengthens.

Sunday's OPEC+ meeting will test the rebound

OPEC+ ministers meet on 29 November, with producers expected to consider keeping current output targets through the first quarter of 2027.

US data offer a reason for caution. Commercial crude inventories rose 1.1 million barrels last week to 418.9 million, the third consecutive increase, although stocks remain roughly 3% below their five-year seasonal average.

ING strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in research carried by FXStreet that recovering US drilling and projected output growth could partly offset Middle Eastern disruptions.

The EIA expects US production to rise from 13.86 million barrels a day this year to 14.3 million in 2027.

Goldman Sachs likewise expects Brent to average $88 next year and ease towards $78 late in 2027 if major supply infrastructure escapes lasting damage.

A return above $100 is possible if immediate supplies tighten. Sustained inventory growth or improving Gulf shipments, however, could make this week's rebound temporary.

data.title: Samsung, SK Hynix stocks surge: why smart money sees a buying opportunity
data.description:
Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix stocks rallied on Friday as bargain hunters returned to South Korean semiconductor stocks following a turbulent week of trading.

Samsung rose 3.91% and SK Hynix gained 4.08%, helping lift the benchmark KOSPI by 3.52%.

The recovery comes as some global fund managers increase their exposure to the chipmakers, despite lingering concerns about memory oversupply and the sustainability of artificial intelligence infrastructure spending.

Samsung, SK Hynix shares: Institutional investors return to battered chip stocks

Jupiter Asset Management has modestly increased its holdings in both companies this week, even as uncertainty surrounding the broader technology sector persists.

“Valuations do look extremely cheap in some of our tech stocks,” Sam Konrad, an Asian equities investment manager at Jupiter, told the Financial Times.

The fund manager also identified signs of market capitulation.

Both chipmakers have lost more than half their value from their recent peaks, leaving investors questioning whether the sell-off has gone too far.

Meanwhile, foreign investors had bought a net 852.3 billion won of KOSPI shares by early afternoon, while individual investors were net sellers of 1.12 trillion won.

SK Hynix was also the most heavily net-bought stock among Mirae Asset Securities clients whose investment returns ranked in the top 1% over the preceding month, the Seoul Economic Daily reported.

Are Samsung and SK Hynix stocks too cheap to ignore?

The scale of the correction looks particularly striking when measured against the chipmakers' recent financial performance.

Samsung reported third-quarter operating profit of 107.4 trillion won, while SK Hynix earned 83.33 trillion won in operating profit on revenue of 104.62 trillion won.

At Wednesday's closing prices, Samsung and SK Hynix traded at just 2.29 and 2.01 times projected 2027 earnings.

Even if earnings were half those estimates, both stocks would have traded at less than five times those hypothetical profits.

Daol Investment & Securities analysts Nam Dae-jong and Kim Yeon-mi described the correction as “excessively steep relative to fundamentals”, according to The Herald Business.

The brokerage values Samsung at 300,000 won and SK Hynix at 2 million won.

However, those valuations depend on future profitability. A prolonged memory glut could undermine the earnings estimates that make both companies appear so inexpensive today.

AI demand and shareholder returns could sustain recovery

Long-term customer agreements may offer some protection against the volatility that has historically characterised the memory industry.

SK Hynix has secured agreements covering more than half its production capacity for 2027 and 2028. It also expects HBM4 to become its mainstream high-bandwidth memory product this quarter.

Shareholder distributions offer another potential catalyst. Samsung expects returns of up to 110 trillion won this year, while SK Hynix plans approximately 100 trillion won.

“Between Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, we favor SK hynix, which has already moved ahead with shareholder returns,” Hanwha Investment & Securities strategist Ha Jang-kwon said, according to Korea JoongAng Daily.

Samsung is expected to announce further details of its shareholder-return plans in January.

Nevertheless, rising manufacturing capacity, higher borrowing costs and uncertainty surrounding AI investment could continue to weigh on both stocks.

data.title: Stephen Yiu explains why Nvidia stock isn't out of the woods just yet
data.description:
Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s (NVDA) chief executive was enough to put a potential lawsuit on hold for one shareholder. It hasn’t settled the questions that could still weigh on the stock.

Stephen Yiu, chief investment officer at Blue Whale Capital, told CNBC he was keeping his Nvidia stake unchanged while waiting to see what congressional questioning and ongoing investigations turn up.

His assessment comes as S&P Global Ratings put the chipmaker’s AA credit rating on “negative” watch, citing concerns about management and board oversight.

Huang’s return changed Yiu’s calculus on a lawsuit

“Probably not for the time being,” Yiu said when asked whether he was still considering legal action.

He had weighed that possibility if the leadership turmoil caused lasting damage to Nvidia’s share price. Huang’s quick return narrowed that window.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on 12 November, before confirming on 23 November that its board had voted unanimously to reinstate him as chief executive, president and a director.

For shareholders, those 11 days mattered because they shortened the period in which Nvidia faced an open-ended search for a permanent successor.

The board’s independent investigation is continuing, however. Yiu said he would “sit tight” over the next couple of weeks as more information comes out. That leaves his response to any new disclosures open.

Strong sales give investors a reason to stay put

Yiu said Nvidia’s underlying business was “actually doing quite well” and suggested the share price might already reflect much of the bad news.

The latest earnings support his assessment. Nvidia reported fiscal third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion on Nov. 17, up 103% from a year earlier.

The next risk for shareholders, in Yiu’s view, is another adverse disclosure that forces investors to revisit what they’ve already priced in.

S&P’s move puts that risk in focus. Nvidia retained its AA rating on Nov. 25, but the agency indicated it could lower the rating to AA− within 90 days if governance concerns persist.

Yiu called the decision “prudent.” For equity investors, the watch gives them a specific issue to follow alongside sales growth: how the board responds to questions about its oversight.

Congress could clarify how much risk sits with Nvidia

Yiu described Nvidia as “mission critical” to the US economy. For him, an unresolved question is whether any liability that emerges from the inquiries would fall on Huang personally or on Nvidia as a company.

The distinction matters to shareholders because findings about the company’s own controls could have implications for how Nvidia sells and distributes its chips.

House committee chairs have confirmed that Huang is due for a closed-door interview on Dec. 1 and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter is scheduled for Dec. 2.

Lawmakers are examining how advanced chips may have reached Chinese entities. Yiu said Blue Whale was keeping its position steady based on what it had learned so far.

The interviews could give investors a clearer basis for judging whether the scrutiny reaches Nvidia’s business practices.
